title: Annual research review: Towards a developmental neuroscience of atypical social cognition.

subsections.subsection_title: Early Social Predispositions and Perceptual Foundations
subsections.content:
Accounts of atypical social cognition increasingly begin before explicit social behavior, in the earliest biases that orient the infant toward socially relevant input. Newborns do not encounter the social world as perceptual generalists: they show selective sensitivity to species-typical signals such as biological motion and, over the first months, increasingly tune cortical responses to the human voice, thereby constraining what information is preferentially sampled for later learning ref [2], ref [5]. These early predispositions are best viewed as probabilistic attentional biases rather than fully specified social knowledge, but they provide an important developmental starting point for the construction of social brain networks.

The visual domain offers a particularly clear example. Newborns preferentially orient to upright biological-motion displays over nonbiological motion and over inverted versions, indicating that the detection of animate movement is available at or near birth and is already sensitive to ecologically valid structure ref [2]. This finding aligns with broader proposals that infant perception is scaffolded by evolutionarily prepared detectors for socially relevant dynamics, including face-like configurations and contingent action patterns (Johnson et al., 1991; Reid et al., 2009). Such biases likely increase exposure to agents, actions, and interactional contingencies that later support person perception, action understanding, and social prediction.

At the same time, the perceptual foundations of social cognition should not be reduced to strong nativist claims. The literature on neonatal imitation has become a key cautionary case: comprehensive reappraisal suggests that evidence for a broad, innate imitative competence is weak, with stronger support for experience-dependent accounts in which sensorimotor contingencies and caregiver interaction gradually solve the correspondence problem ref [1]. Likewise, cortical specialization for voices appears to emerge between roughly 4 and 7 months rather than being fully mature at birth ref [5]; convergent infant fNIRS work shows increasing temporal-cortex selectivity for vocal relative to nonvocal sounds during this period (Grossmann et al., 2010; Lloyd-Fox et al., 2012). Together, these findings motivate a developmental framework in which early biases channel input, and subsequent specialization arises through structured experience-dependent tuning.

subsections.subsection_title: Development of the Social Brain
subsections.content:
Development of the social brain is increasingly understood as a process of progressive functional specialization rather than the simple maturational onset of isolated modules. Work in infancy indicates that core nodes later implicated in adult social cognition—including occipitotemporal, temporal, and prefrontal regions—are already partially engaged within the first postnatal months, but their response properties are initially broad and only gradually become more selective for socially relevant inputs such as faces, gaze, actions, and affective signals ref [5], ref [4]. This pattern is consistent with interactive specialization accounts, in which cortical functions emerge through changing interregional interactions rather than through region-by-region activation alone ref [5], ref [4], ref [5].

Evidence from infant ERP, PET, and developmental fMRI studies supports this view. Face-sensitive responses can be detected early, yet they are less sharply tuned than in adults, with broader activation and prolonged developmental refinement of components such as the infant N290 and later N170 ref [5], ref [4], ref [6], ref [7]. Source analyses further suggest early recruitment of fusiform, superior temporal, lateral occipital, and anterior frontal generators, implying that even regions often linked to higher-order social cognition participate early in perceptual social processing ref [4], ref [8]. Across childhood, face-related activation becomes more focal and differentiated, paralleling increasing functional segregation within the social brain network ref [6], ref [9].

A developmental social-brain framework is especially important for understanding atypical trajectories. Johnson and colleagues argue that conditions such as autism may reflect delayed, reduced, or deviant specialization within this network, rather than the absence of a single social module ref [4]. This interpretation aligns with broader models of the "social brain" as a distributed system spanning STS, fusiform cortex, amygdala, and medial/orbitofrontal regions, whose coordinated development supports later abilities in joint attention, action understanding, and mentalizing ref [10], ref [11].

subsections.subsection_title: Neurodevelopmental Variation and Atypical Social Cognition
subsections.content:
A developmental neuroscience of atypical social cognition must explain not only disorder-specific features, but also how variation in early neurodevelopment redirects social learning trajectories. In autism spectrum disorder (ASD), influential developmental accounts argue that marked phenotypic heterogeneity may nevertheless converge on early disruption to social brain specialization, particularly within circuits supporting reciprocal social engagement and social perception ref [6]. Consistent with this view, functional imaging and connectivity studies suggest that atypical social cognition in ASD reflects altered coordination across distributed social brain systems rather than a single focal deficit ref [6], ref [8].

Importantly, this alteration is not uniform. Whole-brain resting-state analyses indicate a selective fractionation of social brain circuitry in ASD, with especially reduced coupling between limbic-affective regions and temporal, parietal, and frontal systems implicated in communication and action understanding; these circuit-level differences also scale with social symptom severity ref [8]. Such findings complement evidence that posterior superior temporal sulcus responses to intentional action and other socially informative biological signals are atypical in ASD, supporting models in which early disruptions to social orienting and reciprocity canalize later-emerging differences in communication and social understanding ref [6], ref [8].

A broader developmental perspective also requires attention to non-ASD pathways into atypical social cognition. Extremely preterm birth is associated with elevated rates of later psychiatric disorder, including social and emotional difficulties, underscoring that perturbations to early brain maturation can increase risk for atypical social outcomes even outside canonical social neurodevelopmental syndromes ref [4]. Taken together, these data argue for a transdiagnostic framework in which atypical social cognition is understood as an emergent property of interacting neural, experiential, and developmental constraints, while preserving the importance of syndrome-specific circuit profiles ref [6], ref [8], ref [4].

subsections.subsection_title: Methodological and Comparative Frameworks for Development
subsections.content:
A developmental neuroscience of social cognition requires methods that treat age-related differences as transformations in process, circuitry, and measurement rather than as simple child–adult contrasts. Developmental neuroimaging signals are difficult to interpret because changes in activation may reflect shifts in neural coding, support processes, vascular physiology, morphology, or task strategy, not merely "maturation" in any straightforward sense ref [9]. More generally, developmental neuroimaging must take "developing" seriously by prioritizing trajectories, intermediate states, and changing network organization over static snapshots of age groups ref [4].

These concerns are especially important in atypical social cognition, where apparent convergence or divergence in behavior may mask distinct developmental routes. Longitudinal and densely sampled cross-sectional designs are therefore preferable to single time-point comparisons, and multimethod approaches can help dissociate temporal dynamics from spatial localization, particularly when studying infants and children for whom motion, anatomy, and hemodynamic coupling differ from adults ref [4]. Computational accounts are also essential, because verbal constructs such as efficiency or focalization often redescribe developmental findings without specifying the computations that have changed ref [9].

A complementary comparative framework is needed to align developmental stages across species. Cross-mammalian models show that many neural events follow a conserved developmental sequence that can be translated across species, while also revealing systematic heterochronies in cortex and retina and differences between precocial and altricial life histories ref [11]. Such scaling is crucial for interpreting animal models of social brain development, because equivalent postnatal ages are rarely equivalent maturational states ref [11]. Together, these methodological principles support a more mechanistic and evolutionarily grounded account of how typical and atypical social cognition emerges.

subsections.subsection_title: Biological Motion and Action-Perception Pathways
subsections.content:
Biological motion provides a particularly informative bridge between low-level perceptual biases and higher-order social understanding, because it supports rapid extraction of animacy, action structure, and intention from sparse kinematic cues. In adults, this capacity reliably recruits posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS), together with motion-sensitive extrastriate cortex and broader action-perception networks [1][2][3]. Developmentally, however, biological motion perception is not simply an early-emerging competence that is neurally mature from infancy onward; rather, sensitivity improves with task demands, especially under noise or masking conditions, indicating prolonged refinement of the mechanisms that integrate local motion with global body form [4][5].

A central developmental proposal is that biological motion depends on the changing balance between ventral and dorsal visual pathways. Consistent with this view, Lichtensteiger et al. reported that 5- to 7-year-old children showed greater engagement of fusiform and middle temporal regions, whereas adults showed stronger right pSTS recruitment during point-light action perception, suggesting that the canonical dorsal-stream/pSTS solution is still immature in early childhood [6]. This interpretation aligns with evidence that dorsal stream functions, including motion and structure-from-motion processing, mature relatively slowly compared with ventral visual functions [7][8], and with accounts of pSTS as a convergence zone linking visual analysis of body movement to socially relevant action representations [9].

These action-perception pathways are especially relevant to atypical social cognition. Impaired recognition of biological motion has been described in autism and after early periventricular lesions, implicating disrupted mapping between perceptual kinematics and social interpretation rather than a unitary deficit in vision alone [10][11]. Framed developmentally, atypical social cognition may therefore arise not only from differences in specialized "social brain" regions, but also from altered maturation of the perceptual and sensorimotor pathways that furnish those regions with structured input about agents, actions, and intentions.

subsections.section_title: Early Infancy and the Emergence of Social Cognition
subsections.subsection_title: From Early Social Cognition to Theory of Mind and Attachment
subsections.content:
Early social cognition emerges within the first year as infants become increasingly organized around persons as intentional and regulatory partners. By late infancy, selective attachment is evident in proximity seeking, separation protest, and use of the caregiver as a secure base for exploration and a safe haven under stress, indicating that social understanding is already embedded in dyadic regulation rather than in isolated cognitive skills ref [14], ref [5]. These early capacities provide a developmental platform for later representational social cognition, but they are not equivalent to mature theory of mind.

The transition from early sensitivity to goals, emotions, and contingent interaction toward explicit belief reasoning is protracted. A landmark meta-analysis of false-belief performance showed a robust developmental shift across the preschool years, with performance moving from below-chance in younger children to reliably above-chance by around 4 years, despite task variations and cross-cultural sampling ref [13]. This pattern supports genuine conceptual change in understanding mental representations rather than a mere release from task demands, while remaining compatible with the view that earlier infancy supplies foundational competences in joint attention, social expectation, and person-centered learning ref [3], ref [4].

Attachment relationships likely shape this trajectory indirectly by organizing infants’ opportunities for emotion regulation, social learning, and mental-state discourse. Caregiver sensitivity predicts attachment security, and parental reflective capacities and attachment representations are linked to children’s attachment organization and later socio-emotional adjustment ref [14], ref [6], ref [7]. Conversely, disorganized attachment and severe deprivation are associated with elevated risk for later dysregulation and psychopathology ref [14], ref [8]. Thus, from a developmental neuroscience perspective, attachment and theory of mind should be treated as partially distinct but deeply interacting pathways through which early social experience scaffolds atypical and typical social cognition.

subsections.section_title: Early Infancy and the Emergence of Social Cognition
subsections.subsection_title: Emotion Processing and Social Referencing in Infancy
subsections.content:
Emotion processing in infancy develops from broad sensitivity to affective valence toward more differentiated use of others’ signals in regulating action. Infants discriminate emotional expressions in face and voice during the first postnatal months, but the meaning of these cues for behavior is initially limited and context dependent. A functionalist perspective is especially useful here because it emphasizes not only perceptual discrimination, but the infant’s emerging ability to use others’ emotions to guide exploration, avoidance, and proximity seeking ref [15]. At the same time, work on infant facial expressions cautions against assuming a one-to-one mapping between observed facial configurations and discrete internal emotions, underscoring that early emotion processing is organized, dynamic, and only gradually differentiated ref [4].

By the end of the first year, social referencing becomes a key mechanism through which infants use caregivers’ affect to resolve ambiguity. Classic visual-cliff studies showed that maternal emotional signals regulate crossing behavior, with positive signals promoting approach and negative signals inhibiting it. Subsequent work indicates that this process is not purely visual: in 12-month-olds, vocal cues can be as effective as, and in some cases more effective than, facial cues in guiding behavior, suggesting that the voice is a particularly potent channel for early social appraisal ref [17]. Related studies with novel toys and ambiguous objects similarly show increased looking to caregivers, reduced approach under fearful or disgusted signals, and context-sensitive modulation of exploration, establishing social referencing as a bridge between emotion perception and action selection.

Importantly, infants’ responses are often more robust for valence than for discrete negative emotions. Reviews of differential responding suggest that clear functional specificity for anger, fear, sadness, and disgust emerges only gradually across the second year, even though laboratory discrimination can be demonstrated earlier ref [15]. This distinction matters for atypical development: disruptions in attention to affective cues, integration of facial and vocal information, or using others’ emotion to regulate behavior could alter the developmental pathway from early social appraisal to later social understanding. Emotion processing and social referencing in infancy therefore provide an early window onto how social cognition becomes behaviorally meaningful, and why its developmental timing may be critical for identifying atypical trajectories ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Early Infancy and the Emergence of Social Cognition
subsections.subsection_title: Early Social Attention and Communicative Engagement
subsections.content:
Early social attention is organized around infants’ growing sensitivity to cues that signal communicative relevance. One particularly robust marker is the infant’s own name: by around 4–5 months, infants preferentially orient to the sound pattern of their own name, suggesting that selective attention is already being tuned by socially meaningful auditory signals rather than by low-level novelty alone ref [19]. Such early sensitivity likely scaffolds later communicative engagement by helping infants detect when speech is directed to them.

A second core development is the shift from dyadic engagement to triadic coordination. Experimental work indicates that even 3-month-olds distinguish an adult who merely looks away from one who alternates attention between infant and object, with greater smiling and social looking in the latter case, implying an early sensitivity to triadic attention structure ref [20]. This finding complements gaze-following studies showing that young infants can orient toward attended targets under supportive conditions, although the efficiency and flexibility of such attention sharing improve across the first year (e.g., D’Entremont et al., 1997; Hood et al., 1998; Carpenter et al., 1998).

These early behavioral signatures are developmentally important because joint attention is not unitary. Later work distinguishes responding to others’ bids from initiating bids oneself, with partially separable neural systems: responding recruits regions linked to social interpretation, whereas initiating additionally engages fronto-parietal control circuitry, while both rely on medial prefrontal and posterior superior temporal regions associated with shared attention states ref [5]. Developmental accounts similarly argue that atypicalities in social attention and communicative engagement may arise from disruptions in the coordination of orienting, affective engagement, and emerging social-cognitive control (Mundy & Newell, 2007; Mundy et al., 2000; Brooks & Meltzoff, 2005).

subsections.section_title: Early Infancy and the Emergence of Social Cognition
subsections.subsection_title: Neural and Developmental Bases of Emerging Social Cognition
subsections.content:
Emerging social cognition in infancy depends on the rapid organization of distributed neural systems that support orienting, affective evaluation, and the interpretation of socially informative cues. Meta-analytic work in adults identifies a core frontoparietal-temporal network linking eye movements, covert attention, and gaze perception, including intraparietal, precentral, and superior temporal regions, thereby providing an important systems-level template for developmental accounts of early social attention ref [21]. Developmental models further suggest that these cortical networks are assembled in interaction with subcortical and frontolimbic circuitry early in life, rather than appearing fully specified at birth (Johnson, 2001; Johnson, 2005; Grossmann & Johnson, 2007).

Infant studies increasingly support this view. Functional measures indicate early sensitivity to joint attention and gaze-object congruency over frontal and medial prefrontal regions in the first year, implying that neural specialization for socially directed attention is already underway before robust behavioral competence is fully expressed (Senju, Johnson, & Csibra, 2006; Grossmann & Johnson, 2010; Mundy, Card, & Fox, 2000). Structural evidence adds a crucial developmental dimension: white-matter microstructure in the right uncinate fasciculus at 6 months predicts individual differences in responding to joint attention at 9 months, implicating right-lateralized frontolimbic pathways connecting ventromedial prefrontal cortex, anterior temporal regions, and amygdala in the emergence of triadic engagement ref [4].

These findings are especially relevant for atypical development because they suggest that early perturbations in connectivity may alter the developmental trajectory of later social-cognitive skills, including joint attention, attachment-related regulation, and eventually theory-of-mind capacities. More broadly, they argue for a developmental neuroscience of social cognition that links infant behavior to age-sensitive changes in brain organization, while remaining cautious about interpreting infant neuroimaging signals and cross-age continuity too directly (Nelson, Thomas, & de Haan, 2006; Dehaene-Lambertz, Dehaene, & Hertz-Pannier, 2002; Johnson et al., 2005).

subsections.subsection_title: Deprivation, Attachment Disorder, and Developmental Risk
subsections.content:
Studies of children exposed to profound early institutional deprivation have been central in distinguishing attachment disorder from both normative attachment insecurity and more general psychopathology. Follow-up of the English and Romanian Adoptees cohort showed a graded association between duration of deprivation and disinhibited attachment behavior, including indiscriminate sociability and poor checking back with caregivers, with substantial persistence from 4 to 6 years after adoption into supportive families ref [1]. Related work from this cohort further demonstrated that severe deprivation was associated not only with attachment disturbance but also with broader patterns of cognitive delay and social atypicality, indicating that atypical social development can emerge from adverse early environments through multiple pathways rather than a unitary deficit ref [2], ref [3].

This literature was important in shaping later distinctions between reactive attachment disorder and disinhibited social engagement/disinhibited attachment patterns. Observational and interview-based studies in previously institutionalized children suggested that indiscriminate friendliness may persist despite improved caregiving and can be partly dissociable from attachment security assessed in standard paradigms ref [4], ref [5]. At the same time, deprivation is not deterministic: even among severely deprived children, outcomes are heterogeneous, implying moderation by timing, duration, child characteristics, and post-adoption environment ref [1], ref [6].

From a developmental-neuroscience perspective, these findings identify early neglect as a potent risk context for atypical social cognition because it alters the expected calibration of selective social approach, social reciprocity, and caregiver-specific regulation. Intervention studies reinforce this interpretation: placement into family care markedly improves outcomes, but earlier placement is associated with better attachment organization and fewer indiscriminate social behaviors, consistent with sensitive-period accounts of social brain development ref [7], ref [8]. Thus, attachment disorder behavior following deprivation is best viewed as a developmental risk marker that both indexes pathogenic social experience and forecasts broader vulnerability in attention, peer relations, and later psychopathology ref [1], ref [9].

subsections.subsection_title: Neurodevelopmental Effects of Early Neglect and Intervention Timing
subsections.content:
Evidence from children exposed to severe psychosocial neglect indicates that early deprivation alters the maturation of neural systems supporting attention and cognitive engagement. Institutional rearing has been associated with an EEG profile marked by elevated low-frequency power and reduced alpha/beta power, a pattern often interpreted as delayed cortical maturation rather than merely transient state effects (Marshall et al., 2004; ref [23]). Convergent neuroimaging work in previously institutionalized children further points to reduced glucose metabolism, altered white-matter connectivity, and smaller cerebellar volume following early deprivation (Chugani et al., 2001; Eluvathingal et al., 2006; Bauer et al., 2009).

The strongest causal evidence comes from the Bucharest Early Intervention Project, in which placement into high-quality foster care partially normalized later brain function. Although intervention effects were not evident on EEG at 42 months (Marshall et al., 2008), by 8 years children assigned to foster care showed higher alpha power than children remaining in care-as-usual institutions, especially over central regions, and those placed before 24 months displayed alpha activity approximating never-institutionalized peers ref [23]. This timing effect is consistent with earlier BEIP findings that cognitive recovery is also greatest when family placement occurs earlier in development (Nelson et al., 2007), supporting the view that at least some neural consequences of neglect are experience-dependent and sensitive to intervention timing.

At a broader developmental level, these findings suggest that atypical social cognition following neglect may partly arise from altered calibration of large-scale cortical systems during an early sensitive period. Longitudinal studies of severely deprived Romanian adoptees similarly show persistent effects of early privation, but also meaningful heterogeneity in outcome as a function of duration of deprivation and subsequent rearing quality (O'Connor et al., 2000; Beckett et al., 2006; Rutter et al., 2007). For developmental neuroscience, the implication is not simply that neglect causes deficit, but that the timing, duration, and remediation of adverse care shape risk trajectories through their effects on neural plasticity.

subsections.subsection_title: Early Autism Risk Markers in Infancy
subsections.content:
Prospective infant-sibling studies have shifted the search for autism risk markers from retrospective parental report to direct observation of developmental change in the first year. Synthesizing early work, behavioral signs are typically subtle at 6 months but become more discriminable by 12 months, especially in domains central to social orienting and communicative engagement ref [24], ref [3], ref [4]. Reported markers include reduced eye contact and social smiling, poorer orienting to name, atypical visual tracking and attentional disengagement, diminished imitation, altered reactivity and social interest, emerging sensory-focused behaviors, and early receptive/expressive language delays ref [24], ref [5], ref [6].

A key developmental point is that risk may be indexed less by a single pathognomonic sign than by atypical trajectories across multiple social-attentional systems. In Zwaigenbaum and colleagues’ high-risk cohort, no robust overall behavioral separation was evident at 6 months, whereas by 12 months a cluster of markers prospectively differentiated infants later diagnosed with autism from other siblings and low-risk controls ref [24]. This trajectory-based view is consistent with other sibling studies showing that declines in eye fixation across the first 2 years, atypical response to name by the end of the first year, and emerging social-communication differences jointly improve prediction beyond any isolated marker ref [5], ref [7], ref [8].

Neurophysiological work suggests that these behavioral changes are paralleled by altered early social brain function. Using fNIRS at 6–7 months, infants at familial high risk showed differences in the magnitude, timing, and spatial distribution of responses to facial identity and emotion, despite broadly similar waveform shapes to controls, implying atypical specialization rather than a total absence of face sensitivity ref [25]. Convergent ERP work similarly reports altered neural responses to faces and eye gaze in high-risk infants, supporting the idea that autism risk involves early perturbation of face-processing and salience-detection networks that may precede overt clinical symptoms ref [9], ref [10]. Overall, infancy findings favor a developmental-cascade account in which early disruptions in attention to socially relevant cues constrain later social learning.

subsections.subsection_title: Attachment, Autism, and Internalizing Risk
subsections.content:
Attachment provides an important bridge between early social atypicality and later affective risk. In autism, attachment security is not precluded by core social-communication impairments: the meta-analysis by Rutgers et al. found that many children with autism show organized attachment behavior, with roughly half classified as secure, although overall security is moderately reduced relative to comparison groups, especially in samples with more marked cognitive impairment or more strictly defined autism ref [26]. This argues against older views that autism entails an absence of attachment, and instead supports models in which autism and attachment are partially dissociable but developmentally interacting ref [26].

That interaction may be especially relevant for internalizing trajectories. Across development, insecure attachment is reliably associated with anxiety, with meta-analytic evidence indicating a moderate overall relation and particularly strong links for ambivalent/preoccupied forms of insecurity ref [27]. Because anxious attachment strategies amplify vigilance to caregiver availability and uncertainty, they may compound the social unpredictability and emotion-regulation difficulties already faced by some autistic children. Emerging reviews of attachment in autism similarly suggest that variation in caregiver sensitivity and in the child’s attachment organization may help explain heterogeneity in later emotional outcomes, rather than constituting a simple by-product of autistic symptom severity ref [26].

A developmental-neuroscience perspective therefore benefits from treating attachment and autism as intersecting dimensions of risk. Not all autistic children are insecurely attached, and not all insecurity confers the same liability; however, when atypical social attention and communication co-occur with insecure attachment representations, the risk for internalizing symptoms may increase, particularly as social demands intensify across childhood and adolescence ref [26], ref [27]. This framing also highlights a practical implication: interventions that support caregiver sensitivity, co-regulation, and the child’s sense of interpersonal safety may be relevant not only for relationship quality, but also for downstream anxiety risk.

subsections.section_title: Later Developmental Progression of Social Cognition
subsections.subsection_title: Neural Systems and Adolescent Reorganization of Social Processing
subsections.content:
Adolescence is increasingly viewed as a period of reorganization, rather than simple linear maturation, in neural systems supporting social information processing. Longitudinal morphometric work indicates continued remodeling of core “social brain” regions—including medial prefrontal cortex, temporoparietal junction, posterior superior temporal sulcus, and anterior temporal cortex—well into the early twenties, with regionally specific declines in cortical thickness and grey matter volume suggestive of prolonged circuit refinement ref [30]. These structural changes parallel developmental shifts in functional recruitment during mentalizing and self–other evaluation, consistent with the idea that adolescent social cognition depends on reweighted interactions among distributed cortical and subcortical systems.

A second component of adolescent reorganization concerns incentive and affective salience. Reviews of developmental reward processing emphasize that ventral striatal and orbitofrontal responses to reward cues and outcomes are still changing during adolescence, with social contexts often amplifying these effects ref [4]. Dopaminergic accounts further propose that age-related variation in mesolimbic signaling transiently heightens incentive motivation, novelty seeking, and sensitivity to peer-related rewards during this period ref [29]. Such models help explain why social acceptance, status, and exclusion become unusually powerful regulators of attention and behavior in adolescence, even when regulatory prefrontal systems are still maturing ref [29], ref [4].

For atypical development, the key implication is that adolescent social difficulties may reflect altered coordination between social-perceptual, mentalizing, and reward-control circuits rather than isolated deficits in a single module. Neurodevelopmental models therefore increasingly focus on frontostriatal–social brain coupling, pubertal timing, and experience-dependent plasticity as mechanisms through which vulnerability to psychopathology may emerge during adolescence ref [29], ref [30], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Later Developmental Progression of Social Cognition
subsections.subsection_title: Social Cognition in Psychopathology and Antisocial Development
subsections.content:
A developmental account of psychopathology increasingly treats atypical social cognition as a mechanism linking early neural bias to later disorder. In antisocial development, conduct problems are heterogeneous, with distinct pathways to predominantly reactive aggression versus the more severe callous-unemotional profile marked by reduced sensitivity to others’ distress cues ref [33]. Functional imaging studies in youths with disruptive behavior and callous-unemotional traits consistently implicate diminished amygdala engagement to fear, alongside weaker amygdala–ventromedial prefrontal coupling, suggesting atypical processing of socially salient signals that normally support empathy, aversive learning, and moral socialization ref [31], ref [34].

This pattern appears relatively specific: compared with youths with ADHD, those with callous-unemotional traits show reduced amygdala response to fearful, but not necessarily angry, expressions, supporting the view that antisocial behavior can arise from separable neurocognitive routes rather than a unitary disorder ref [31], ref [33]. By contrast, anxiety-related psychopathology is often characterized by heightened responsivity to socially threatening cues. Preliminary longitudinal evidence indicates that greater amygdala reactivity to angry and even neutral faces predicts adolescent social anxiety symptoms, suggesting that altered calibration of threat-processing systems can foreshadow maladaptive social evaluation biases ref [6].

A broader lesson is that social-cognitive dysfunction is transdiagnostic, but not uniform. In schizophrenia, social cognition encompasses partly dissociable domains—including theory of mind, social perception, attributional style, and emotion processing—that relate to symptoms and everyday functioning, while requiring developmentally sensitive measurement ref [35]. Across disorders, then, atypical social cognition is best understood not as a single deficit, but as disorder-specific perturbations in how maturing neural systems encode affective cues, infer intentions, and regulate social behavior ref [33], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Later Developmental Progression of Social Cognition
subsections.subsection_title: From Imitation to Early Mental-State Understanding
subsections.content:
Imitation and early pretend play have often been treated as developmental precursors to explicit mental-state reasoning, but contemporary accounts emphasize that these links are neither linear nor reducible to a single innate mechanism. Work on infancy has challenged strong nativist readings of neonatal imitation, arguing instead that imitative competence is shaped by rich sensorimotor and social experience, including repeated contingencies between seeing and doing actions ref [1]. At the same time, imitation is not purely instrumental: it serves affiliative and communicative functions, with children copying more faithfully when social belonging or interpersonal alignment is at stake ref [37]. This social embedding is important for developmental neuroscience accounts because it places early action understanding within reciprocal interaction rather than isolated perceptual matching.

Pretence provides a more direct bridge to mental-state understanding. Leslie’s influential account proposed that pretend play reflects an emerging capacity for metarepresentation, allowing the child to decouple representations from current reality and thereby to understand both one’s own and others’ pretend states ref [36]. In this view, the appearance of object substitution and imaginary scenarios in the second year marks an early form of representing representations, foreshadowing later theory-of-mind performance. Consistent with this developmental continuity, meta-analytic evidence indicates that explicit false-belief understanding shows a reliable developmental progression across the preschool years, with substantial gains between ages 3 and 5 years and continued refinement thereafter.

Importantly, mental-state understanding does not stop with first-order false belief. Children’s grasp of recursive or second-order mental states—reasoning about what one person thinks about another person’s belief—emerges later, typically around 5 to 7 years, and predicts more advanced social interpretation, including irony, deception, and strategic communication ref [8]. This later-developing competence is mirrored at the neural level: theory-of-mind performance in childhood correlates with increasing functional specialization of right temporo-parietal cortex for thinking about thoughts, beyond more general social information ref [9]. Together, these findings suggest a prolonged developmental trajectory from socially situated imitation and pretence toward increasingly explicit, recursive, and neurally specialized mental-state reasoning ref [37] ref [1] ref [8] ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Later Developmental Progression of Social Cognition
subsections.subsection_title: Development of Social Emotions, Empathy, and Moral Evaluation
subsections.content:
Social emotions emerge early but become increasingly differentiated as children integrate affective experience with representations of social relationships and standards. Jealousy can be observed in infancy and becomes more clearly organized across the second and third years as children track triadic relations and threats to valued bonds, illustrating that some social emotions precede explicit verbal mental-state reasoning ref [40]. Guilt likewise shows a measurable developmental course in the toddler and preschool years: behavioral and affective signs of post-transgression discomfort are already coherent and moderately stable by the second year, and are linked to temperament, parenting, and later rule compliance ref [45].

Development also involves qualitative change in how children represent emotions. For social emotions in particular, children increasingly rely on scripts that privilege causes and consequences over facial expressions alone, with embarrassment, shame, and compassion differentiated later than basic emotions ref [7]. This pattern suggests that mature social-emotional understanding depends on integrating appraisals of agency, norm violation, reputation, and interpersonal context rather than decoding expressions in isolation. Such findings align with neurodevelopmental work showing that moral sensitivity is supported by interacting affective and cognitive systems: younger children show stronger salience-related responses to others' harm, whereas with age judgments of intent and deserved punishment become more differentiated and increasingly recruit ventromedial prefrontal circuitry involved in integrating outcome and intention information ref [8].

Adolescence appears to be a key period for reorganization of social-emotional processing. Functional imaging studies indicate that thinking about guilt and embarrassment recruits the mentalizing network in both adolescents and adults, but adolescents rely relatively more on anterior medial prefrontal regions, whereas adults show greater temporal-pole engagement, consistent with a shift toward more distributed and efficient social-semantic processing ref [9]. Within early adolescence, pubertal maturation contributes additional variance beyond chronological age: higher gonadal and adrenal hormone levels are associated with greater anterior temporal activity during social-emotion processing, while age itself predicts reduced dorsomedial prefrontal recruitment ref [10]. Together, these findings support a developmental neuroscience account in which empathy, self-conscious emotion, and moral evaluation arise from the progressive integration of affective salience, social knowledge, and mental-state inference across childhood and adolescence ref [45], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Later Developmental Progression of Social Cognition
subsections.subsection_title: Atypical Social Cognition in Autism and Related Neurodevelopmental Conditions
subsections.content:
Autism spectrum conditions provide an important test case for atypical social cognition, but the literature increasingly suggests specificity rather than global social failure. On explicit theory-of-mind tasks, able autistic individuals can sometimes perform adequately, yet spontaneous mental-state attribution remains reduced, as shown by the absence of anticipatory false-belief looking in Asperger syndrome despite intact performance on standard verbal tasks ref [48]. Similarly, when mental states must be inferred from animated shapes, autistic participants give fewer and less accurate mentalistic descriptions and show reduced recruitment of medial prefrontal, temporo-parietal, and temporal regions within the broader mentalizing network ref [53].

This heterogeneity is also evident in social communication and affect reading. In autism, pragmatic difficulties are closely linked to theory of mind, and comparison work with fragile X syndrome indicates that the most marked impairments in social communication and mental-state reasoning occur in idiopathic autism and fragile X with comorbid autism, rather than fragile X alone ref [47]. Neuroimaging studies of irony and communicative intent further show reduced medial prefrontal and superior temporal responses in autistic children, although explicit instructions to attend to face and voice cues can partially normalize activity, implying atypical spontaneous orienting rather than complete incapacity ref [50].

A similar reframing has emerged for empathy and emotion. Reduced self-referential cognition and alexithymia are common in autism and predict poorer mentalizing and more autistic traits ref [46]. However, the 'alexithymia hypothesis' argues that many putative emotional deficits in autism are driven by co-occurring alexithymia rather than autism itself ref [9]; consistent with this, empathic insula responses track alexithymia levels but not autism diagnosis ref [10]. Beyond mentalizing and empathy, diminished social motivation may also affect strategic social behaviour: autistic adolescents show reduced flattery and reputation management, and individual differences in social enjoyment predict these effects ref [13]. Together, these findings argue for parsing autism-related social difficulties into partially dissociable components—spontaneous mentalizing, social motivation, and alexithymia-linked affective awareness—rather than treating atypical social cognition as a unitary deficit.

subsections.subsection_title: Integrating Social Cognition and Self-Referential Processing
subsections.content:
A key challenge for developmental accounts of atypical social cognition is to integrate mentalizing with self-referential processing, rather than treating them as separable domains. Converging work suggests that representations of one’s own mental and affective states scaffold inferences about other minds, with overlap in cortical midline and temporo-parietal systems supporting both self-related thought and theory of mind in typical development and autism alike [1]. This view is broadly consistent with simulation-based accounts, but also implies that atypical social cognition may partly reflect altered access to, or organization of, self-related representations rather than a unitary theory-of-mind deficit alone [1].

Evidence from autism supports this integration directly. In adults with autism spectrum conditions, self-referential memory effects are present but attenuated, and reduced self-referential processing covaries with poorer mentalizing and greater autistic traits; alexithymia and self-focused attention further modulate these associations [1]. Such findings suggest that difficulties in understanding others may be linked to atypical encoding of one’s own internal states, especially in domains where emotional awareness and self-monitoring are required. This interpretation also helps explain why performance can vary across tasks that differ in their demands on introspection, emotion labeling, and explicit reflection.

Developmental neuroimaging extends this framework by showing that neural specialization for thinking about minds continues to sharpen across childhood. In particular, children’s theory-of-mind performance correlates with increasing functional selectivity of the right temporo-parietal junction for mental-state reasoning, indicating that behavioral gains are tied to the refinement of social-cognitive circuitry rather than mere age-related improvement [4]. Integrating these findings with evidence on self-referential processing suggests a productive agenda for future work: to trace how mPFC, precuneus, and TPJ jointly support the developing interface between self-knowledge and social inference, and how disruption of this interface may generate distinct autistic phenotypes [1,4].

subsections.subsection_title: Emotion, Empathy, and Individual Differences
subsections.content:
A key advance in recent work is the recognition that atypical social cognition cannot be reduced to a unitary empathy deficit. In autism, affective responding appears to vary substantially as a function of co-occurring alexithymia, with empathic responses in anterior insula tracking alexithymic traits rather than diagnostic status per se [1]. This reframes apparent impairments in affect sharing as, at least in part, consequences of altered interoceptive and emotion-labeling capacities, consistent with evidence that alexithymia contributes importantly to the emotional symptoms often attributed globally to autism [1].

At the behavioral level, individual differences in emotion processing extend beyond empathy to the regulation of one's own affect. Adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism report elevated negative affect, greater difficulty identifying and describing feelings, reduced habitual use of cognitive reappraisal, and lower reappraisal self-efficacy, even when differences in affective experience are controlled [2]. These findings suggest that difficulties in perspective shifting may constrain adaptive regulation strategies, while reliance on suppression may reflect compensatory but less flexible control styles [2].

Taken together, these results argue for models of atypical social cognition that explicitly separate mentalizing, affect sharing, interoception, and emotion regulation, while also accounting for substantial within-diagnosis heterogeneity. Individual differences in alexithymia and regulatory style may help explain why some autistic individuals show relatively preserved empathic resonance despite social-communicative difficulties, whereas others present broader affective vulnerabilities [1,2]. This emphasis on dimensional variation has clear translational implications, pointing toward stratified assessment and interventions that target emotion awareness and reappraisal rather than assuming a uniform social-emotional impairment.

subsections.subsection_title: Developmental Trajectories and Behavioral Phenotypes
subsections.content:
A developmental-neuroscience account of atypical social cognition must explain not only mean group differences, but also how early biases canalize into distinct behavioral phenotypes across time. Prospective work suggests that atypical trajectories can emerge very early: by age two, autistic toddlers fail to show the normative preference for biological motion and instead orient to non-social audiovisual contingencies, implying that early social input may be sampled in qualitatively different ways [2]. Such findings support cascade models in which small differences in attention to socially informative stimuli accumulate into broader differences in social learning, communication, and adaptive behavior.

At the phenotypic level, heterogeneity within neurodevelopmental conditions is equally important. Newson and colleagues argued that pathological demand avoidance represents a distinguishable profile within pervasive developmental disorders, marked by socially strategic demand avoidance, mood lability, role-play strengths, and a different sex ratio from classic autism [1]. Whether or not PDA is ultimately treated as a discrete nosological entity, the broader lesson is that developmental pathways may diverge into behaviorally meaningful subtypes that are poorly captured by unitary spectrum models alone [1]. This perspective aligns with contemporary efforts to parse autism-related heterogeneity in terms of developmental mechanisms rather than only symptom totals.

More broadly, childhood behavioral style appears to have transdiagnostic significance for later social adaptation. In a population cohort, a gradient of childhood self-control predicted adult health, wealth, and criminal offending, even after accounting for IQ and social class, and sibling-comparison analyses suggested that these effects were not reducible to shared family background [3]. For atypical social cognition research, such findings argue that longitudinal phenotypes should integrate social-attentional biases, regulatory control, and motivational style. Future studies will benefit from linking early neural markers to developmental trajectories that cut across diagnostic boundaries and forecast clinically relevant outcomes [2,3].

subsections.subsection_title: Neural and Translational Frameworks for Future Directions
subsections.content:
A key priority for future developmental neuroscience is to move beyond case-control descriptions toward mechanistic and translational models that link neural variation to risk, resilience, and treatment response. In autism, neuroimaging work has already suggested that atypical social brain function can be decomposed into state, trait, and compensatory signatures, with biological-motion responses in pSTS, fusiform, amygdala, and medial prefrontal systems offering one candidate endophenotypic architecture for stratification ref [59]. This framework is especially valuable because unaffected siblings may show neural atypicalities despite near-typical behavior, implying that brain-based measures may capture liability and compensation more sensitively than symptom counts alone ref [59].

Such approaches should be integrated with developmental designs that take age-related changes in neural signal seriously and that constrain heterogeneity at the circuit level rather than the diagnostic level alone ref [34], ref [41]. More broadly, work on the emergence of the social brain network and infant social brain development suggests that longitudinal, multimodal markers spanning perception, reward, and self-referential processing will be necessary to chart divergent developmental pathways before full behavioral phenotypes consolidate ref [49], ref [51]. Cross-species developmental modeling may further help align sensitive periods and circuit maturation across animal and human studies, thereby improving causal inference and translational relevance ref [32].

The translational promise of this agenda is underscored by experimental work in Rett syndrome showing that delayed restoration of MeCP2 can reverse marked neurological and electrophysiological abnormalities in mice, even after symptom onset ref [3]. Although Rett syndrome is etiologically distinct from idiopathic autism, this finding is conceptually important for atypical social cognition because it demonstrates that severe neurodevelopmental phenotypes need not be irreversibly fixed by early development ref [3]. Together, circuit-level endophenotypes in humans and reversible mechanistic models in animals motivate a future framework in which biomarkers are used not only to classify heterogeneity, but also to identify windows of plasticity, monitor intervention effects, and test whether compensatory neural pathways can be deliberately strengthened ref [59], ref [55].
